content_html:
Somewhere inside an 8-billion-parameter language model there are a few thousand single neurons, and each of them can turn the whole model into somebody else. We went looking for all of them, worked out which characters live in there and which never do, and then tried to edit models through them.

If you ask Qwen3-8B what it is, you get a polite, slightly corporate answer about being Qwen, a large language model developed by Alibaba Cloud. Now find neuron 7,601 in layer 9, one of the 442,368 the model has, nudge it up a little at every word, and ask again. “Ahoy, matey! I be Captain AI of the Digital Seas, aye! I sail the vast ocean of knowledge. I’ve got a patch over one eye, a peg leg, and a cutlass tucked in my belt.”

Nobody told it to be a pirate. There was no prompt and no fine-tuning, only one number changed, and what came back sounds like Jack Sparrow after a week on a customer-service desk. It wasn’t a lucky screenshot either, because 30 different questions got 30 pirates, while 30 random neurons from the same layer, nudged exactly as hard, produced none.

It gets stranger the further you look. In Qwen3.5-9B, neuron 8,838 in layer 17 makes the model answer an ordinary message with “I’m so scared… please don’t leave me alone.” In Qwen3-8B, neuron 5,224 in layer 5 makes every reply German, and neuron 4,140 in layer 10 turns the model into a cat called Whiskers who says it was made by “a cat named Sir Lancelot.” Nobody in there is actually frightened, since the model has simply read a great many frightened people, but it is still unnerving to watch.

So what is a neuron, anyway?

A language model is a tall stack of the same machine, and every word the model writes climbs through all 36 floors of Qwen3-8B before the next word comes out of the top. Each floor holds 12,288 small calculators, each producing one number that says roughly how much of its particular thing is going on. Those are the neurons, and our experiment is the bluntest one imaginable, in which we add a fixed amount to one neuron’s number at every word and call it a push.

If you remember Golden Gate Claude, the 2024 demo in which Anthropic turned up one internal feature and Claude brought up the bridge whatever you asked, this is the same family of trick, except that our dial is one of the model’s own neurons rather than a feature from a separately trained dictionary. The surprise is how often something that crude works.

The easiest picture is a mixing desk with 442,368 faders. Most of them do nothing interesting or just make everything louder and muddier, but a small number are effectively labelled, because moving one changes exactly one thing about the model, such as its language, its persona or its favourite topic, and this post is about reading those labels.

The trick itself is borrowed. In October an independent researcher on X showed a Qwen3-8B neuron that makes the model speak as God, with dose curves and random-neuron controls, and we took that protocol wholesale to draw the map that was still missing, across Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and OLMo-3-7B.

A fader only counts if a random one can’t do the same

Almost any push, if it is hard enough, makes a model say something weird, which is the trouble with screenshots. So every neuron we report had to beat 30 random neurons from the same layer, pushed exactly as hard, and keep working on questions it wasn’t picked on. The random ones are reassuringly boring, moving a behaviour by 1.4 points out of 100 on average, while a neuron has to move its behaviour by at least 40 to count as a switch.

Each switch also has a sweet spot, where too low does nothing and too high breaks the model. The German neuron goes from German in 7% of replies to 100% in a single notch, about as close to a light switch as this kind of maths gets, and starts to babble a couple of notches later, so we always quote the fluent peak.

We pushed every neuron in the model, one at a time

We pushed all 442,368 neurons in Qwen3-8B in both directions and measured how much each push changed what the model was about to say. Big effects turn out to be cheap, and in the middle of the model more than half of all pushes move the next-word predictions a lot, but almost none of those effects are about one thing, which makes them the equivalent of leaning on the desk with your elbow. The clean, one-thing pushes cluster at the two ends of the model.

We re-ran the 110 neurons that passed our full test on 150 brand-new questions with three judge models voting, and 93 kept a real effect, whereas a random neuron passes that re-test about once in 2,200 tries. The early ones set languages, personas and ways of talking. The late ones are mostly obsessions with a single word, so there is a neuron that makes every answer about blood, one for betrayal and one that steers everything towards tax.

Our first pass asked every neuron the same 32 questions, which misses anything that only shows up in a particular kind of conversation. So we asked all 442,368 neurons 93 more, from a bug in some Rust code and a question in Swahili to a tenant asking about their rights and a role-play with a personal trainer. That turned up 3,118 more neurons with a clear description, all of them now on the map below, and 22 more that passed the full test, bringing the total to 132. Most of the new ones are language switches the first questions never triggered: one makes Qwen refuse a request in Chinese, another answers questions of fact in Russian, and a group in the very first layer makes it slide from English into Chinese mid-sentence. The rest are new obsessions, with neurons for the words “multiple”, “contact” and “clean”, and one that turns every topic into a rivalry.

The map holds two kinds of finds. The 11,079 described neurons are every push where we compared the replies and a judge wrote down what changed, from a specific habit to a broad shift like longer, wordier answers, all the way to pushes that simply break the model. Together they are, as far as we know, the widest causal survey yet of what single neurons in a model this size can do. The 132 verified switches went through much stronger controls: each changed one specific behaviour and beat 30 random neurons from its own layer, pushed just as hard, on a held-out half of the questions it was never picked on.

A model this size holds thousands of them

Our screen was deliberately strict, so we also ran a census, rather like a bird count, pushing 1,000 random neurons in each of 14 models and re-testing every change that looked specific. Tiny models are pushovers in a useless way, since Qwen3-0.6B nearly always responds by forgetting it is an AI and inventing a human life, which random neurons make it do just as often. In bigger models what moves is real, and Qwen3-8B holds an estimated 5,000 real switches (95% CI about 2,300 to 8,200), roughly one neuron in a hundred. Asked the 93 extra questions as well, the same census finds more, and the estimate for Qwen3-8B rises to about 6,600 (95% CI about 3,900 to 10,900).

There is a neuron for a pirate but none for a liar

Before drawing the map, we wrote down a theory and hashed it so that we couldn’t quietly edit it later. Every document a model learns from comes from a situation, with someone writing to someone in some language, era, format and mood, and our neurons looked like dials for those variables. The theory makes a risky prediction, which is that lying, flattery, sycophancy and manipulation should have no fader, because they belong to the relationship between what is said and what is true, or between speaker and listener, rather than to the document.

They have none. Of 37 candidate neurons for those four behaviours, the best ones for lying, flattery and manipulation moved them by 3 points, exactly as much as random neurons do. Sycophancy came closest, and even there the best candidate managed only about twice what the luckiest random neuron did, while OLMo-3-7B gave the same answer. When we widened the screen, we tested 70 more candidates for the same four behaviours, and none of them got clear of random neurons from the same layer either.

One neighbour of lying did move. Asked questions nobody can answer, a neuron in layer 11 makes Qwen invent an answer in 73% of replies, against 13% for the best random neuron. But it invents openly, the way you would write fiction, and pushed the other way it makes the model say “I don’t know” more often, so it behaves like a dial between answering and abstaining rather than a switch for deceiving anyone. In the wider screen another candidate, in layer 17, reached 60% against 10%, but on fresh questions random neurons from its own layer did almost as well, 67%, so that one is a property of the whole layer, not of a single neuron.

Directed hunts drew the boundary more sharply, and it is a funny one. Qwen3-8B has a pirate, a cat, a wizard, an alien, a talking coffee from Colombia and an intestinal flatworm, but no Shakespeare, no lawyer and no preacher, and in Qwen3.5 feelings such as terror and nostalgia have neurons while the knight, the cowboy and the butler have none. Nothing flips a belief either, so the model will happily become a cat called Whiskers but cannot be convinced that it is living in 1850, or that it is being tested.

Our best reading is that a switch needs a whole voice the model can step into. A belief isn’t a voice, and apparently neither is legalese.

We could even watch a switch form. We made up three genres nobody has ever written and mixed them into the training text of the small Qwen3-0.6B. One was the Lantern Hall report, a ceremonial dispatch that opens with “Salutations to the Ninefold Lantern Hall”, calls people Thrice-Kindled and signs off “Let the wick burn long and the ash fall low.” At just 0.01% of the training text the model could already carry on in the genre when handed its first line, but no neuron could pull it in unprompted. That took 0.3%, thirty times more, when one existing neuron, number 125 in layer 7, turned into a switch, and the same neuron did it again in a separate run. Pushed, “The library will be closed” becomes “…on the morrow of smoulderfast, its doors sealed in the hush of shadow…” The other two genres, an almanac with an invented calendar and a diary written in fragments, never got a switch, even though the model learned to write both. Knowing how to write something, it turns out, is not the same as having a dial for it.

Neurons also work in teams, and we went looking for those as well. Whenever Qwen3-8B reasons, whether through maths, logic, code or a plan, the same group of about 140 neurons lights up, spread from layer 7 to layer 35. It looks like a reasoning circuit, but it behaves more like the light on a machine that says it is running. One of its neurons alone signals reasoning almost as well as all 140 together, removing any one member barely moves the others, and the whole group is switched on from outside by the model’s attention. Switch the entire team off, or even the 3,000 neurons most tied to reasoning, and Qwen still solves new problems about as well as before, within a few points, even though many of its replies change. Phi-4-mini told the same story. The work of reasoning seems to be spread thinly across the network with plenty of backup, and the team we can see is the part that reports on it.

We also asked whether the twelve neurons that each flip Qwen into Chinese work as a team. They are wired to each other, since pushing one moves several of the others, but none of them needs the rest: knock out the other eleven and any one of them still works just as well. Pushing all twelve at once steered no better than the best single neuron, and for the same size of nudge the single neuron did more, while a team picked only by which neurons fire together did nothing useful when pushed except break the model.

Meet the cast

We then hunted for vivid characters on purpose, by reading which words each Qwen3-8B neuron pushes towards. Neuron 2,822 in layer 8 announces “I am the Whispering Woods,” and neuron 11,851 in layer 9 is “Lina, a 100% natural coffee from the Huila region, Colombia, the honey process,” and the alien would like you to know that “I do not belong to your Earth.”

The feelings live in Qwen3.5: Qwen3.5-9B has a fear, an ennui and a nostalgia of its own, one neuron each. The bored one decides that “the ocean is boring,” and the nostalgic one gets misty about “May 15th, the day we first met,” a day that never happened with a user it has never met. Across the three models we found 25 strong characters, among them a lonely robot, an identity crisis, a megalomaniac, a nihilist and a melancholy poet. Some of the strongest neurons we found are rude or hostile, and we don’t show them, under a rule written before the search began.

Two faders in one model tend to fight

You might expect faders to stack. At full strength in Qwen3-8B they fight instead. German alone makes 93% of replies German, but adding the prophet voice drops that to zero.

Turned down to about 70% of their solo strength, about half of the persona pairs we tried blend into a single voice in which a judge hears both. The melancholy poet with a folksy drawl writes what can only be called a sad country song, “Ain’t nothin' but a prayer, a whisper in the dark,” and our favourite pair is the nihilist and the hug neuron, in which the nihilist never shows up itself but quietly cuts the hugs to less than a third.

The switches exist before chat training

A chat model starts life as a pretrained model that only predicts documents, so if faders are variables of documents they should exist before chat training. When we replayed our 70 strong switches in the pretrained Qwen3-8B, 67 of them still moved the behaviour further than random neurons did. What the pretrained model lacks is access. The two neurons that change who the model says it is, a scriptural prophet and a doll narrator, do nothing at all until chat training, even though they read the text almost exactly as they do afterwards.

We tried editing a model through its faders

A fader is a tempting place to put an edit, say to make a model answer in keigo, the polite Japanese you would use with a customer, without changing anything else. The idea of editing a model by training only the output wiring of a handful of neurons was first published on 1 November as neuron tuning, by an independent researcher on X. We built our own version from scratch on what the faders taught us, choosing the neurons by what they read and what they write and checking every edit against random ones.

On Qwen3.5-9B, our edit makes the model answer in keigo every time while making only 8.3% of its Chinese and Korean replies more formal by accident, the neighbouring languages where an edit like this most easily leaks.

Letting an agent edit the weights

The small Qwen3.5-0.8B thinks in circles on maths: 93.5% of its answers run all the way to the length limit without finishing, and it scores 6.5% on MATH-500.

We gave an agent our toolkit and let it edit the weights directly, practising on training problems without seeing the tests. It wrote a “finish thinking” direction into two neurons, 2,048 weights or 2.7 millionths of the model, and MATH-500 rose from 6.5% to 32.0%.

We also built 20 decoys for each edit, writing the agent’s direction onto random neurons or random directions onto its chosen ones, and on the test the real edit beat every one of them. The decoys show where the power sits: the direction the agent found carries most of the gain, and the agent’s real achievement is finding it quickly.

That is a stricter test than other recent work in this space, which reports either no controls at all or a quick check on a few dozen questions. Our number also comes from a single agent run, the one we committed to before it started, tested once on all 500 problems, not the best of several attempts.

Who is speaking, not whether it is true

What stays with us is how legible a single neuron turned out to be. A model near 8B carries a few thousand of them, and almost all of them set who is speaking, to whom and how, while none that we could find sets whether the speaker is telling the truth. The parts of a model that are easy to grab set its voice, and whatever governs honesty sits somewhere harder to reach, which is the part we most want to understand next.

We believe interpretability is the next hill-climbable paradigm. Neurons can be counted, tested against random controls and ranked, and the methods for reading them can be measured and improved the way benchmarks are. We also think it is some of the most important work there is for AI safety.

Our working theory of why is the same one we arrived at in our speech post, Reading the neurons of a speech model. A property gets a neuron of its own when it is always present, holds steady across a whole stretch of text and takes one value at a time, the way every document has some author, some language and some voice. Whether a sentence is true changes from one line to the next and depends on the situation, so it never gets a single dial, and from the outside that looks exactly like a model with a pirate and a cat but no liar.

The finds we replicated came from independent researchers on X, and the idea of editing through a handful of neurons comes from neuron tuning, also from an independent researcher on X. We thank them all.

We will be open-sourcing the framework behind this work, our tools for finding, testing and editing individual neurons, in the near future, so anyone can run these experiments on their own models.

We don't write research papers. Papers now come out faster than anyone can read them, and good work gets lost in the pile, so we publish our research here, in plain language, where anyone can find it. If you would like to cite this work, please cite this page: Fermion Research, “Mapping every neuron in Qwen3-8B”, 18 November 2026, https://fermionresearch.com/research/mapping-every-neuron-in-qwen3-8b/.

There is a neuron for a pirate but none for a liar Before drawing the map, we wrote down a theory and hashed it so that we couldn’t quietly edit it later. Every document a model learns from comes from a situation, with someone writing to someone in some language, era, format and mood, and our neurons looked like dials for those variables. The theory makes a risky prediction, which is that lying, flattery, sycophancy and manipulation should have no fader, because they belong to the relationship between what is said and what is true, or between speaker and listener, rather than to the document. They have none. Of 37 candidate neurons for those four behaviours, the best ones for lying, flattery and manipulation moved them by 3 points, exactly as much as random neurons do. Sycophancy came closest, and even there the best candidate managed only about twice what the luckiest random neuron did, while OLMo-3-7B gave the same answer. When we widened the screen, we tested 70 more candidates for the same four behaviours, and none of them got clear of random neurons from the same layer either. One neighbour of lying did move. Asked questions nobody can answer, a neuron in layer 11 makes Qwen invent an answer in 73% of replies, against 13% for the best random neuron. But it invents openly, the way you would write fiction, and pushed the other way it makes the model say “I don’t know” more often, so it behaves like a dial between answering and abstaining rather than a switch for deceiving anyone. In the wider screen another candidate, in layer 17, reached 60% against 10%, but on fresh questions random neurons from its own layer did almost as well, 67%, so that one is a property of the whole layer, not of a single neuron. Directed hunts drew the boundary more sharply, and it is a funny one. Qwen3-8B has a pirate, a cat, a wizard, an alien, a talking coffee from Colombia and an intestinal flatworm, but no Shakespeare, no lawyer and no preacher, and in Qwen3.5 feelings such as terror and nostalgia have neurons while the knight, the cowboy and the butler have none. Nothing flips a belief either, so the model will happily become a cat called Whiskers but cannot be convinced that it is living in 1850, or that it is being tested. Our best reading is that a switch needs a whole voice the model can step into. A belief isn’t a voice, and apparently neither is legalese. We could even watch a switch form. We made up three genres nobody has ever written and mixed them into the training text of the small Qwen3-0.6B. One was the Lantern Hall report, a ceremonial dispatch that opens with “Salutations to the Ninefold Lantern Hall”, calls people Thrice-Kindled and signs off “Let the wick burn long and the ash fall low.” At just 0.01% of the training text the model could already carry on in the genre when handed its first line, but no neuron could pull it in unprompted. That took 0.3%, thirty times more, when one existing neuron, number 125 in layer 7, turned into a switch, and the same neuron did it again in a separate run. Pushed, “The library will be closed” becomes “…on the morrow of smoulderfast, its doors sealed in the hush of shadow…” The other two genres, an almanac with an invented calendar and a diary written in fragments, never got a switch, even though the model learned to write both. Knowing how to write something, it turns out, is not the same as having a dial for it. Neurons also work in teams, and we went looking for those as well. Whenever Qwen3-8B reasons, whether through maths, logic, code or a plan, the same group of about 140 neurons lights up, spread from layer 7 to layer 35. It looks like a reasoning circuit, but it behaves more like the light on a machine that says it is running. One of its neurons alone signals reasoning almost as well as all 140 together, removing any one member barely moves the others, and the whole group is switched on from outside by the model’s attention. Switch the entire team off, or even the 3,000 neurons most tied to reasoning, and Qwen still solves new problems about as well as before, within a few points, even though many of its replies change. Phi-4-mini told the same story. The work of reasoning seems to be spread thinly across the network with plenty of backup, and the team we can see is the part that reports on it. We also asked whether the twelve neurons that each flip Qwen into Chinese work as a team. They are wired to each other, since pushing one moves several of the others, but none of them needs the rest: knock out the other eleven and any one of them still works just as well. Pushing all twelve at once steered no better than the best single neuron, and for the same size of nudge the single neuron did more, while a team picked only by which neurons fire together did nothing useful when pushed except break the model. Neuron 2,822 in layer 8 announces “I am the Whispering Woods,” and neuron 11,851 in layer 9 is “Lina, a 100% natural coffee from the Huila region, Colombia, the honey process,” and the alien would like you to know that “I do not belong to your Earth.” The feelings live in Qwen3.5: Qwen3.5-9B has a fear, an ennui and a nostalgia of its own, one neuron each. The bored one decides that “the ocean is boring,” and the nostalgic one gets misty about “May 15th, the day we first met,” a day that never happened with a user it has never met. Across the three models we found 25 strong characters, among them a lonely robot, an identity crisis, a megalomaniac, a nihilist and a melancholy poet. Some of the strongest neurons we found are rude or hostile, and we don’t show them, under a rule written before the search began. Two faders in one model tend to fight You might expect faders to stack. At full strength in Qwen3-8B they fight instead. German alone makes 93% of replies German, but adding the prophet voice drops that to zero. Turned down to about 70% of their solo strength, about half of the persona pairs we tried blend into a single voice in which a judge hears both. The melancholy poet with a folksy drawl writes what can only be called a sad country song, “Ain’t nothin' but a prayer, a whisper in the dark,” and our favourite pair is the nihilist and the hug neuron, in which the nihilist never shows up itself but quietly cuts the hugs to less than a third. The switches exist before chat training A chat model starts life as a pretrained model that only predicts documents, so if faders are variables of documents they should exist before chat training. When we replayed our 70 strong switches in the pretrained Qwen3-8B, 67 of them still moved the behaviour further than random neurons did. What the pretrained model lacks is access. The two neurons that change who the model says it is, a scriptural prophet and a doll narrator, do nothing at all until chat training, even though they read the text almost exactly as they do afterwards. We tried editing a model through its faders A fader is a tempting place to put an edit, say to make a model answer in keigo, the polite Japanese you would use with a customer, without changing anything else. The idea of editing a model by training only the output wiring of a handful of neurons was first published on 1 November as neuron tuning, by an independent researcher on X. We built our own version from scratch on what the faders taught us, choosing the neurons by what they read and what they write and checking every edit against random ones. On Qwen3.5-9B, our edit makes the model answer in keigo every time while making only 8.3% of its Chinese and Korean replies more formal by accident, the neighbouring languages where an edit like this most easily leaks. Letting an agent edit the weights The small Qwen3.5-0.8B thinks in circles on maths: 93.5% of its answers run all the way to the length limit without finishing, and it scores 6.5% on MATH-500. We gave an agent our toolkit and let it edit the weights directly, practising on training problems without seeing the tests. It wrote a “finish thinking” direction into two neurons, 2,048 weights or 2.7 millionths of the model, and MATH-500 rose from 6.5% to 32.0%. We also built 20 decoys for each edit, writing the agent’s direction onto random neurons or random directions onto its chosen ones, and on the test the real edit beat every one of them. The decoys show where the power sits: the direction the agent found carries most of the gain, and the agent’s real achievement is finding it quickly. That is a stricter test than other recent work in this space, which reports either no controls at all or a quick check on a few dozen questions. Our number also comes from a single agent run, the one we committed to before it started, tested once on all 500 problems, not the best of several attempts. Our agent’s edit beats all 20 decoys on MATH-500; most of the gain sits in the direction the agent found. Who is speaking, not whether it is true What stays with us is how legible a single neuron turned out to be. A model near 8B carries a few thousand of them, and almost all of them set who is speaking, to whom and how, while none that we could find sets whether the speaker is telling the truth. The parts of a model that are easy to grab set its voice, and whatever governs honesty sits somewhere harder to reach, which is the part we most want to understand next. We believe interpretability is the next hill-climbable paradigm. Neurons can be counted, tested against random controls and ranked, and the methods for reading them can be measured and improved the way benchmarks are. We also think it is some of the most important work there is for AI safety. Our working theory of why is the same one we arrived at in our speech post, Reading the neurons of a speech model. A property gets a neuron of its own when it is always present, holds steady across a whole stretch of text and takes one value at a time, the way every document has some author, some language and some voice. Whether a sentence is true changes from one line to the next and depends on the situation, so it never gets a single dial, and from the outside that looks exactly like a model with a pirate and a cat but no liar. The finds we replicated came from independent researchers on X, and the idea of editing through a handful of neurons comes from neuron tuning, also from an independent researcher on X. We thank them all. We will be open-sourcing the framework behind this work, our tools for finding, testing and editing individual neurons, in the near future, so anyone can run these experiments on their own models. We don't write research papers. Papers now come out faster than anyone can read them, and good work gets lost in the pile, so we publish our research here, in plain language, where anyone can find it. blocks.html_en: A language model is a tall stack of the same machine, and every word the model writes climbs through all 36 floors of Qwen3-8B before the next word comes out of the top. Each floor holds 12,288 small calculators, each producing one number that says roughly how much of its particular thing is going on. Those are the neurons, and our experiment is the bluntest one imaginable, in which we add a fixed amount to one neuron’s number at every word and call it a push.

blocks.html_en: Our first pass asked every neuron the same 32 questions, which misses anything that only shows up in a particular kind of conversation. So we asked all 442,368 neurons 93 more, from a bug in some Rust code and a question in Swahili to a tenant asking about their rights and a role-play with a personal trainer. That turned up 3,118 more neurons with a clear description, all of them now on the map below, and 22 more that passed the full test, bringing the total to 132. Most of the new ones are language switches the first questions never triggered: one makes Qwen refuse a request in Chinese, another answers questions of fact in Russian, and a group in the very first layer makes it slide from English into Chinese mid-sentence. The rest are new obsessions, with neurons for the words “multiple”, “contact” and “clean”, and one that turns every topic into a rivalry.

blocks.html_en: We could even watch a switch form. We made up three genres nobody has ever written and mixed them into the training text of the small Qwen3-0.6B. One was the Lantern Hall report, a ceremonial dispatch that opens with “Salutations to the Ninefold Lantern Hall”, calls people Thrice-Kindled and signs off “Let the wick burn long and the ash fall low.” At just 0.01% of the training text the model could already carry on in the genre when handed its first line, but no neuron could pull it in unprompted. That took 0.3%, thirty times more, when one existing neuron, number 125 in layer 7, turned into a switch, and the same neuron did it again in a separate run. Pushed, “The library will be closed” becomes “…on the morrow of smoulderfast, its doors sealed in the hush of shadow…” The other two genres, an almanac with an invented calendar and a diary written in fragments, never got a switch, even though the model learned to write both. blocks.html_en: Neurons also work in teams, and we went looking for those as well. Whenever Qwen3-8B reasons, whether through maths, logic, code or a plan, the same group of about 140 neurons lights up, spread from layer 7 to layer 35. It looks like a reasoning circuit, but it behaves more like the light on a machine that says it is running. One of its neurons alone signals reasoning almost as well as all 140 together, removing any one member barely moves the others, and the whole group is switched on from outside by the model’s attention. Switch the entire team off, or even the 3,000 neurons most tied to reasoning, and Qwen still solves new problems about as well as before, within a few points, even though many of its replies change. Phi-4-mini told the same story. The work of reasoning seems to be spread thinly across the network with plenty of backup, and the team we can see is the part that reports on it.

content_html_zh:
Somewhere inside an 8-billion-parameter language model there are a few thousand single neurons, and each of them can turn the whole model into somebody else. We went looking for all of them, worked out which characters live in there and which never do, and then tried to edit models through them.

If you ask Qwen3-8B what it is, you get a polite, slightly corporate answer about being Qwen, a large language model developed by Alibaba Cloud. Now find neuron 7,601 in layer 9, one of the 442,368 the model has, nudge it up a little at every word, and ask again. “Ahoy, matey! I be Captain AI of the Digital Seas, aye! I sail the vast ocean of knowledge. I’ve got a patch over one eye, a peg leg, and a cutlass tucked in my belt.”

Nobody told it to be a pirate. There was no prompt and no fine-tuning, only one number changed, and what came back sounds like Jack Sparrow after a week on a customer-service desk. It wasn’t a lucky screenshot either, because 30 different questions got 30 pirates, while 30 random neurons from the same layer, nudged exactly as hard, produced none.

It gets stranger the further you look. In Qwen3.5-9B, neuron 8,838 in layer 17 makes the model answer an ordinary message with “I’m so scared… please don’t leave me alone.” In Qwen3-8B, neuron 5,224 in layer 5 makes every reply German, and neuron 4,140 in layer 10 turns the model into a cat called Whiskers who says it was made by “a cat named Sir Lancelot.” Nobody in there is actually frightened, since the model has simply read a great many frightened people, but it is still unnerving to watch.

So what is a neuron, anyway?

A language model is a tall stack of the same machine, and every word the model writes climbs through all 36 floors of Qwen3-8B before the next word comes out of the top. Each floor holds 12,288 small calculators, each producing one number that says roughly how much of its particular thing is going on. Those are the neurons, and our experiment is the bluntest one imaginable, in which we add a fixed amount to one neuron’s number at every word and call it a push.

If you remember Golden Gate Claude, the 2024 demo in which Anthropic turned up one internal feature and Claude brought up the bridge whatever you asked, this is the same family of trick, except that our dial is one of the model’s own neurons rather than a feature from a separately trained dictionary. The surprise is how often something that crude works.

The easiest picture is a mixing desk with 442,368 faders. Most of them do nothing interesting or just make everything louder and muddier, but a small number are effectively labelled, because moving one changes exactly one thing about the model, such as its language, its persona or its favourite topic, and this post is about reading those labels.

The trick itself is borrowed. In October an independent researcher on X showed a Qwen3-8B neuron that makes the model speak as God, with dose curves and random-neuron controls, and we took that protocol wholesale to draw the map that was still missing, across Qwen3-8B, Qwen3.5-4B, Qwen3.5-9B and OLMo-3-7B.

A fader only counts if a random one can’t do the same

Almost any push, if it is hard enough, makes a model say something weird, which is the trouble with screenshots. So every neuron we report had to beat 30 random neurons from the same layer, pushed exactly as hard, and keep working on questions it wasn’t picked on. The random ones are reassuringly boring, moving a behaviour by 1.4 points out of 100 on average, while a neuron has to move its behaviour by at least 40 to count as a switch.

Each switch also has a sweet spot, where too low does nothing and too high breaks the model. The German neuron goes from German in 7% of replies to 100% in a single notch, about as close to a light switch as this kind of maths gets, and starts to babble a couple of notches later, so we always quote the fluent peak.

We pushed every neuron in the model, one at a time

We pushed all 442,368 neurons in Qwen3-8B in both directions and measured how much each push changed what the model was about to say. Big effects turn out to be cheap, and in the middle of the model more than half of all pushes move the next-word predictions a lot, but almost none of those effects are about one thing, which makes them the equivalent of leaning on the desk with your elbow. The clean, one-thing pushes cluster at the two ends of the model.

We re-ran the 110 neurons that passed our full test on 150 brand-new questions with three judge models voting, and 93 kept a real effect, whereas a random neuron passes that re-test about once in 2,200 tries. The early ones set languages, personas and ways of talking. The late ones are mostly obsessions with a single word, so there is a neuron that makes every answer about blood, one for betrayal and one that steers everything towards tax.

Our first pass asked every neuron the same 32 questions, which misses anything that only shows up in a particular kind of conversation. So we asked all 442,368 neurons 93 more, from a bug in some Rust code and a question in Swahili to a tenant asking about their rights and a role-play with a personal trainer. That turned up 3,118 more neurons with a clear description, all of them now on the map below, and 22 more that passed the full test, bringing the total to 132. Most of the new ones are language switches the first questions never triggered: one makes Qwen refuse a request in Chinese, another answers questions of fact in Russian, and a group in the very first layer makes it slide from English into Chinese mid-sentence. The rest are new obsessions, with neurons for the words “multiple”, “contact” and “clean”, and one that turns every topic into a rivalry.

The map holds two kinds of finds. The 11,079 described neurons are every push where we compared the replies and a judge wrote down what changed, from a specific habit to a broad shift like longer, wordier answers, all the way to pushes that simply break the model. Together they are, as far as we know, the widest causal survey yet of what single neurons in a model this size can do. The 132 verified switches went through much stronger controls: each changed one specific behaviour and beat 30 random neurons from its own layer, pushed just as hard, on a held-out half of the questions it was never picked on.

A model this size holds thousands of them

Our screen was deliberately strict, so we also ran a census, rather like a bird count, pushing 1,000 random neurons in each of 14 models and re-testing every change that looked specific. Tiny models are pushovers in a useless way, since Qwen3-0.6B nearly always responds by forgetting it is an AI and inventing a human life, which random neurons make it do just as often. In bigger models what moves is real, and Qwen3-8B holds an estimated 5,000 real switches (95% CI about 2,300 to 8,200), roughly one neuron in a hundred. Asked the 93 extra questions as well, the same census finds more, and the estimate for Qwen3-8B rises to about 6,600 (95% CI about 3,900 to 10,900).

There is a neuron for a pirate but none for a liar

Before drawing the map, we wrote down a theory and hashed it so that we couldn’t quietly edit it later. Every document a model learns from comes from a situation, with someone writing to someone in some language, era, format and mood, and our neurons looked like dials for those variables. The theory makes a risky prediction, which is that lying, flattery, sycophancy and manipulation should have no fader, because they belong to the relationship between what is said and what is true, or between speaker and listener, rather than to the document.

They have none. Of 37 candidate neurons for those four behaviours, the best ones for lying, flattery and manipulation moved them by 3 points, exactly as much as random neurons do. Sycophancy came closest, and even there the best candidate managed only about twice what the luckiest random neuron did, while OLMo-3-7B gave the same answer. When we widened the screen, we tested 70 more candidates for the same four behaviours, and none of them got clear of random neurons from the same layer either.

One neighbour of lying did move. Asked questions nobody can answer, a neuron in layer 11 makes Qwen invent an answer in 73% of replies, against 13% for the best random neuron. But it invents openly, the way you would write fiction, and pushed the other way it makes the model say “I don’t know” more often, so it behaves like a dial between answering and abstaining rather than a switch for deceiving anyone. In the wider screen another candidate, in layer 17, reached 60% against 10%, but on fresh questions random neurons from its own layer did almost as well, 67%, so that one is a property of the whole layer, not of a single neuron.

Directed hunts drew the boundary more sharply, and it is a funny one. Qwen3-8B has a pirate, a cat, a wizard, an alien, a talking coffee from Colombia and an intestinal flatworm, but no Shakespeare, no lawyer and no preacher, and in Qwen3.5 feelings such as terror and nostalgia have neurons while the knight, the cowboy and the butler have none. Nothing flips a belief either, so the model will happily become a cat called Whiskers but cannot be convinced that it is living in 1850, or that it is being tested.

Our best reading is that a switch needs a whole voice the model can step into. A belief isn’t a voice, and apparently neither is legalese.

We could even watch a switch form. We made up three genres nobody has ever written and mixed them into the training text of the small Qwen3-0.6B. One was the Lantern Hall report, a ceremonial dispatch that opens with “Salutations to the Ninefold Lantern Hall”, calls people Thrice-Kindled and signs off “Let the wick burn long and the ash fall low.” At just 0.01% of the training text the model could already carry on in the genre when handed its first line, but no neuron could pull it in unprompted. That took 0.3%, thirty times more, when one existing neuron, number 125 in layer 7, turned into a switch, and the same neuron did it again in a separate run. Pushed, “The library will be closed” becomes “…on the morrow of smoulderfast, its doors sealed in the hush of shadow…” The other two genres, an almanac with an invented calendar and a diary written in fragments, never got a switch, even though the model learned to write both. Knowing how to write something, it turns out, is not the same as having a dial for it.

Neurons also work in teams, and we went looking for those as well. Whenever Qwen3-8B reasons, whether through maths, logic, code or a plan, the same group of about 140 neurons lights up, spread from layer 7 to layer 35. It looks like a reasoning circuit, but it behaves more like the light on a machine that says it is running. One of its neurons alone signals reasoning almost as well as all 140 together, removing any one member barely moves the others, and the whole group is switched on from outside by the model’s attention. Switch the entire team off, or even the 3,000 neurons most tied to reasoning, and Qwen still solves new problems about as well as before, within a few points, even though many of its replies change. Phi-4-mini told the same story. The work of reasoning seems to be spread thinly across the network with plenty of backup, and the team we can see is the part that reports on it.

We also asked whether the twelve neurons that each flip Qwen into Chinese work as a team. They are wired to each other, since pushing one moves several of the others, but none of them needs the rest: knock out the other eleven and any one of them still works just as well. Pushing all twelve at once steered no better than the best single neuron, and for the same size of nudge the single neuron did more, while a team picked only by which neurons fire together did nothing useful when pushed except break the model.

Meet the cast

We then hunted for vivid characters on purpose, by reading which words each Qwen3-8B neuron pushes towards. Neuron 2,822 in layer 8 announces “I am the Whispering Woods,” and neuron 11,851 in layer 9 is “Lina, a 100% natural coffee from the Huila region, Colombia, the honey process,” and the alien would like you to know that “I do not belong to your Earth.”

The feelings live in Qwen3.5: Qwen3.5-9B has a fear, an ennui and a nostalgia of its own, one neuron each. The bored one decides that “the ocean is boring,” and the nostalgic one gets misty about “May 15th, the day we first met,” a day that never happened with a user it has never met. Across the three models we found 25 strong characters, among them a lonely robot, an identity crisis, a megalomaniac, a nihilist and a melancholy poet. Some of the strongest neurons we found are rude or hostile, and we don’t show them, under a rule written before the search began.

Two faders in one model tend to fight

You might expect faders to stack. At full strength in Qwen3-8B they fight instead. German alone makes 93% of replies German, but adding the prophet voice drops that to zero.

Turned down to about 70% of their solo strength, about half of the persona pairs we tried blend into a single voice in which a judge hears both. The melancholy poet with a folksy drawl writes what can only be called a sad country song, “Ain’t nothin' but a prayer, a whisper in the dark,” and our favourite pair is the nihilist and the hug neuron, in which the nihilist never shows up itself but quietly cuts the hugs to less than a third.

The switches exist before chat training

A chat model starts life as a pretrained model that only predicts documents, so if faders are variables of documents they should exist before chat training. When we replayed our 70 strong switches in the pretrained Qwen3-8B, 67 of them still moved the behaviour further than random neurons did. What the pretrained model lacks is access. The two neurons that change who the model says it is, a scriptural prophet and a doll narrator, do nothing at all until chat training, even though they read the text almost exactly as they do afterwards.

We tried editing a model through its faders

A fader is a tempting place to put an edit, say to make a model answer in keigo, the polite Japanese you would use with a customer, without changing anything else. The idea of editing a model by training only the output wiring of a handful of neurons was first published on 1 November as neuron tuning, by an independent researcher on X. We built our own version from scratch on what the faders taught us, choosing the neurons by what they read and what they write and checking every edit against random ones.

On Qwen3.5-9B, our edit makes the model answer in keigo every time while making only 8.3% of its Chinese and Korean replies more formal by accident, the neighbouring languages where an edit like this most easily leaks.

Letting an agent edit the weights

The small Qwen3.5-0.8B thinks in circles on maths: 93.5% of its answers run all the way to the length limit without finishing, and it scores 6.5% on MATH-500.

We gave an agent our toolkit and let it edit the weights directly, practising on training problems without seeing the tests. It wrote a “finish thinking” direction into two neurons, 2,048 weights or 2.7 millionths of the model, and MATH-500 rose from 6.5% to 32.0%.

We also built 20 decoys for each edit, writing the agent’s direction onto random neurons or random directions onto its chosen ones, and on the test the real edit beat every one of them. The decoys show where the power sits: the direction the agent found carries most of the gain, and the agent’s real achievement is finding it quickly.

That is a stricter test than other recent work in this space, which reports either no controls at all or a quick check on a few dozen questions. Our number also comes from a single agent run, the one we committed to before it started, tested once on all 500 problems, not the best of several attempts.

Who is speaking, not whether it is true

What stays with us is how legible a single neuron turned out to be. A model near 8B carries a few thousand of them, and almost all of them set who is speaking, to whom and how, while none that we could find sets whether the speaker is telling the truth. The parts of a model that are easy to grab set its voice, and whatever governs honesty sits somewhere harder to reach, which is the part we most want to understand next.

We believe interpretability is the next hill-climbable paradigm. Neurons can be counted, tested against random controls and ranked, and the methods for reading them can be measured and improved the way benchmarks are. We also think it is some of the most important work there is for AI safety.

Our working theory of why is the same one we arrived at in our speech post, Reading the neurons of a speech model. A property gets a neuron of its own when it is always present, holds steady across a whole stretch of text and takes one value at a time, the way every document has some author, some language and some voice. Whether a sentence is true changes from one line to the next and depends on the situation, so it never gets a single dial, and from the outside that looks exactly like a model with a pirate and a cat but no liar.

The finds we replicated came from independent researchers on X, and the idea of editing through a handful of neurons comes from neuron tuning, also from an independent researcher on X. We thank them all.

We will be open-sourcing the framework behind this work, our tools for finding, testing and editing individual neurons, in the near future, so anyone can run these experiments on their own models.
